grammar.title: First conditional and future time clauses
grammar.explanation:
We use the **first conditional** for real possibilities in the future. The structure is **if + present simple**, **will / won't + infinitive**.

Never use **will** after **if**. Say "If the sommelier recommends it" — never "If the sommelier will recommend it".

**Unless** means **if not**, and it takes the present simple. We won't serve the degustation unless every amuse-bouche is perfect.

After **when**, **as soon as**, **until**, **before**, and **after**, use the present tense for future meaning. The future marker **will** lives only in the main clause.

The first conditional can also give an order or advice. "If the concoction tastes strange, tell me" is an imperative, not a prediction.
examples: *If* the chef *finishes* her mise en place early, we *will* open on time. (a real future possibility)
We *won't* serve the degustation *unless* every amuse-bouche *is* perfect. (unless = if not)
*If* you *tell* the sommelier your budget, he *will* find a wine with beautiful terroir. (no will after if)
I *will* call you *as soon as* the infusion *is* ready. (present after as soon as)
*If* the concoction *tastes* too strange, *don't* serve it. (imperative, not will)
We *won't* leave *until* everyone *has* tasted the delectable dessert. (present after until)

practice.q: Your friend says: 'If the sommelier will recommend a wine, I'll order it.' What's wrong, and how do you fix it?
practice.a: Never use will after if. Say: 'If the sommelier recommends a wine, I'll order it.'

practice.q: Complete with the right forms: 'We ___ (not leave) until the infusion ___ (be) ready.'
practice.a: 'We won't leave until the infusion is ready.' Use will in the main clause and the present tense after until.
